newsitem.title: USA: SEC charges former Cal Micro executives with fraud.
newsitem.headline: SEC charges former Cal Micro executives with fraud.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday filed charges against three former executives of California Micro Devices Corp., alleging fraud and insider trading for the one-time high-flying technology company.
The SEC complaint alleges former President Surendra Gupta committed fraud by helping inflate California Micro's revenues in its fiscal year ended June 30, 1994.
Two other former plant managers, Bhasker Rao and Ramana Penumarty, were also charged with fraud and insider trading, according to the complaint.
"We absolutely deny the allegation and intend to fight it vigorously," William Goodman, a San Francisco-based attorney and counsel for Gupta, said.
Rao and Penumarty could not be reached, and California Micro Devices Chief Financial Officer John Trewin declined to comment on the matter.
Based in the heart of Silicon Valley in Milpitas, Calif., California Micro makes advanced electronics based on thin film technology that are used in communications and computing equipment.

The charges, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, stem from accounting irregularities that surfaced in the fall of 1994 and led to the restatement of 1994 earnings and the resignations of the three executives, Chairman Chan Desaigoudar and Treasurer Steven Hencke.

The SEC claimed the three executives directed employees to falisify documents to show products had been shipped when in fact they had not. In some cases, the products had not even been manufactured, according to the complaint.
In addition, the SEC alleged Rao and Penumarty sold stock in the company while they knew about the irregularities.
By selling the stock based on non-public information, Rao and Penumarty avoided losses of roughly $70,000 and $58,000, respectively, the SEC claimed.
By August 1994, California Micro Devices's stock traded as high as $22 a share based on strong projected earnings growth.
On Aug. 4 of that year, the company reported a fiscal 1994 net profit of $5 million, or 62 cents a share. But the stock plunged to $13.125 as investor concern arose over charges in its report.

By October, when the company finally disclosed it would have to restate its earnings due to what it described as "possible revenue recognition and accounting issues," the stock was down to $5.25. Eventually it bottomed at $3.875.

In February 1995, after the resignation of its top executives, California Micro Devices finally restated 1994 earnings to reflect a net loss of $15.2 million, or $1.88 a share. Revenues were restated to $30.1 million, down from the previous $45.3 million.
On Thursday, California Micro's stock was at $6.69 on Nasdaq.
